text: This lesson covers two separate but equally practical topics: the native JavaScript string methods you'll use on field values constantly, and the real reason ServiceNow has its own date object instead of relying on JavaScript's built-in Date.

Field values off a GlideRecord are plain strings, so every native method works exactly the way it would anywhere else in JavaScript. Trim strips stray leading or trailing whitespace a user typed into a field, split breaks a string into an array on a delimiter, indexOf checks whether a substring is present by testing for a result other than negative one, replace swaps one piece of text for another, and substring pulls out a slice by position.

Template literals, written with backticks, let you interpolate a value directly into a string using a dollar sign and curly braces, instead of concatenating pieces together with plus signs. The output is identical to concatenation - it's purely about readability, and you'll see template literals constantly in modern server-side scripts going forward.

Native JavaScript Date is tied to whatever time zone the server's engine happens to be running in, which is not the same as the instance's configured time zone or an individual user's profile setting. GlideDateTime exists specifically to fix that. Creating one with no argument gives the current moment in the right time zone, getDisplayValue formats it for showing to a user, addDaysUTC moves it forward by a number of days computed in UTC, and before and after compare two GlideDateTime objects.

The rule of thumb: plain string methods for anything that's genuinely text, GlideDateTime for anything that's a real date or time tied to a record. The moment date math touches a record's date field, native Date is the wrong tool, because it has no idea what time zone that value should be read in.
Next, JSON parsing and serialization - turning a JavaScript object into a string and back, which becomes essential once you start working with REST APIs.
